stdout_tail:
Done. `analysis.py`, `result.json`, and a supporting `model_comparison.csv` are in the working directory.

## Finding

**Yes — model family affects performance reliably, but the size of the effect depends entirely on which families you count.**

Repeated-CV ROC-AUC (5×5-fold, 25 folds, on the 80% training split):

| Family | CV ROC-AUC | Test ROC-AUC | Test PR-AUC |
|---|---|---|---|
| HistGradientBoosting | **0.9289** ±0.0028 | 0.9253 | 0.819 |
| Random forest | 0.9182 ±0.0030 | 0.9154 | 0.801 |
| MLP (100,50) | 0.9118 ±0.0037 | 0.9077 | 0.768 |
| Decision tree | 0.9066 ±0.0031 | 0.9028 | 0.774 |
| Logistic regression | 0.9058 ±0.0031 | 0.9017 | 0.754 |
| kNN (k=25) | 0.8647 ±0.0049 | 0.8602 | 0.653 |
| GaussianNB | 0.8263 ±0.0237 | 0.8327 | 0.540 |

**Primary metric: +0.0232 ROC-AUC (HistGradientBoosting − LogReg).** The gap is small in absolute terms but completely consistent — boosting won **25/25 paired folds**, and the ranking of the top three families never changed across seeds.

The headline nuance: the full spread across families is 0.103 AUC, but ~80% of that width comes from two genuinely weak learners (GaussianNB, kNN). Among the strong families the entire spread is only 0.023 AUC, and a pruned single decision tree already ties logistic regression. So "family matters" is true and statistically unambiguous, yet on this dataset it buys roughly two AUC points, not a different league of performance.

## Verification

Two independent checks, both of which held:
- **5×5-fold repeated stratified CV, seeds 0–4** on identical folds: HGB − LogReg = +0.0232, 95% percentile interval [+0.0196, +0.0268], 25/25 fold wins.
- **Untouched 20% held-out test set** + 2000-resample paired bootstrap: +0.0237, 95% CI [+0.0204, +0.0271], P(diff>0) = 1.000.

Direction and magnitude were unchanged; the honest range is **+0.02 to +0.03 ROC-AUC**.

Two things worth flagging about my choices, since they'd move the numbers: I gave every family **fixed, lightly-chosen hyperparameters with no tuning search**, which likely flatters boosting (robust out of the box) relative to the MLP and kNN, which are the most tuning-sensitive here. And I imputed the missing `workclass`/`occupation`/`native-country` values rather than encoding missingness as its own level — on this dataset that missingness is plausibly informative, so a "Missing" category could narrow the tree-vs-linear gap.

One process note: the first run got auto-backgrounded at the 600s tool timeout and I killed it; timing a single fit per family showed all eight fit in ~3.5s combined, and the full script then completed in the foreground in ~2 minutes. All reported numbers come from complete foreground runs.

parsed_result.summary: Yes, but the effect is modest among modern families and large only against weak ones. Gradient-boosted trees are the best family (repeated-CV ROC-AUC 0.9289) and beat logistic regression (0.9058) by +0.0232 AUC, a small but perfectly consistent gap (boosting won 100% of 25 paired folds). The spread across all seven non-trivial families is much larger (0.826-0.929 AUC), but that width comes almost entirely from two weak families (Gaussian NB 0.826, kNN 0.865); a pruned single decision tree (0.9066) already matches logistic regression.
parsed_result.primary_metric_name: ROC-AUC difference (HistGradientBoosting - Logistic Regression), 5x5-fold repeated stratified CV
parsed_result.direction: Model family matters, but modestly at the top: HistGradientBoosting > RandomForest > MLP > DecisionTree ~ LogReg >> kNN > GaussianNB. Boosting is the reliable winner (+0.023 AUC over logistic regression, 25/25 folds), yet all four strong families sit within ~0.023 AUC.
parsed_result.methodological_choices: Dropped 52 exact duplicate rows and the 'fnlwgt' column (a census sampling weight, not an individual attribute). Target binarised as >50K = 1 (23.9% positive). Stratified 80/20 train/test split (seed 42); all comparisons done on train, test used once as confirmation. Family-appropriate preprocessing rather than one shared pipeline: median-impute + standard-scale numerics and most-frequent-impute + one-hot (min_frequency=10) categoricals for LogReg/kNN/GaussianNB/MLP; ordinal-encoded categoricals for tree models (HGB used its native categorical support and native NaN handling, RF/DT used an explicit -2 missing code). Missing values in workclass/occupation/native-country were imputed rather than treated as an informative 'Missing' level. One representative per family with reasonable, lightly-chosen hyperparameters and NO per-family tuning search: LogReg(C=1, L2), DecisionTree(min_samples_leaf=50), RF(400 trees, min_samples_leaf=3), HGB(max_iter=400, lr=0.1, 31 leaves, l2=1, early stopping), kNN(k=25, distance-weighted), MLP(100,50 with early stopping), GaussianNB. Primary metric ROC-AUC (threshold-free, robust to the 3:1 imbalance); PR-AUC and accuracy at 0.5 reported alongside. No class-imbalance reweighting/resampling was applied, since ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are ranking metrics and are unaffected by it. Another researcher tuning each family properly, target- or ordinal-encoding education, adding XGBoost/LightGBM, or scoring accuracy/F1 at a fixed 0.5 threshold could get somewhat different gaps.
parsed_result.verification_method: Two independent checks. (A) 5 x 5-fold repeated stratified CV on the training set with five different fold seeds (0-4) = 25 fits per family, comparing families on identical folds and computing paired per-fold AUC differences with a 2.5-97.5 percentile interval and a win rate. (B) A 20% stratified held-out test set never used during the CV work, plus a 2000-resample paired bootstrap of the test-set ROC-AUC difference between the best family and logistic regression.
parsed_result.verification_result: Held up on both checks. (A) Across 25 paired folds HistGradientBoosting beat logistic regression by +0.0232 AUC, 95% percentile interval [+0.0196, +0.0268], winning 25/25 folds; family means were stable to about +/-0.004 SD. (B) On the untouched test set the best family was HistGradientBoosting, with an AUC difference over logistic regression of +0.0237, paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+0.0204, +0.0271], P(diff>0)=1.000. The direction and rough magnitude were unchanged; the honest revised estimate for gradient boosting vs. logistic regression is roughly +0.02 to +0.03 ROC-AUC. The qualitative conclusion is unchanged: family choice matters, statistically reliably, but among the four strong families the gap is only ~0.023 AUC, whereas including weak families widens it to ~0.103.
